items.text: In some ways, we are more eager to track down and recover knowledge from the distant past than ever. <break time="0.8s" /> New storage technologies make it possible to preserve texts, images, and music at minimal cost, and social media have made it simpler to share this stored content more widely than ever before. <break time="0.8s" /> Never have previously produced cultural artifacts and practices been as readily available to as many people as they are now. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet, amid this digital abundance of cultural content, older file formats, websites, and entire databases are becoming unreadable at a frightening speed, raising the question of whether we are really so much better at preserving the past than our ancestors were. <break time="0.8s" /> And while the technologies of cultural storage and distribution have changed, the laws governing how culture works, how it is preserved, transmitted, exchanged, and recovered, have not. <break time="0.8s" /> The interplay of preservation and destruction, of loss and recovery, of error and adaptation continues unabated in a world that has put almost all human cultures in constant contact.
